cards.explanation: The answer is the blood Saul shed in killing the Gibeonites. The LORD tells David, "It is because of the blood shed by Saul and his family, because he killed the Gibeonites." Saul was Israel's king before David (1 Samuel 11:15). David sought the face of the LORD, and the LORD gave him the cause. When you're stuck, friends, asking the One who knows beats staring at the empty cookie jar.

The answer is False. The Gibeonites, a remnant of the Amorites, had an oath made concerning them. But Saul, Israel's king before David, "…had sought to kill them," in his zeal for Israel and Judah. The oath was on the books, friends, and Saul went the other way.

The answer is that David asks how he can make amends to them. He says, "What shall I do for you? How can I make amends so that you may bless the inheritance of the LORD?" Notice he asks first and doesn't just announce a plan. Then the Gibeonites get to answer him. Good leaders, friends, ask before they act.

The answer is that David says, "Whatever you ask, I will do for you…" The Gibeonites had just turned down silver and gold, and David still left the door wide open. That's a big promise to make before you've heard the request, friends. I think David wanted to hear them out fully.

The answer is seven of Saul's male descendants. They ask that "…seven of his male descendants be delivered to us…" They're speaking of Saul, the man who consumed them and plotted to exterminate them from every border of Israel. This is a heavy request, friends. They want to hang them before the LORD at Gibeah of Saul.
The answer is True. David agrees, and he says, "I will give them to you…" That's a short answer to a heavy request, friends. It sets up what comes next in the story, and it's a hard one.

The answer is his oath with Jonathan. The text says the king spared Mephibosheth "…because of the oath before the LORD between David and Jonathan son of Saul." Jonathan was Saul's son and David's close friend. Back then Jonathan told David, "…we have sworn friendship with each other in the name of the LORD" (1 Samuel 20:42). David remembered the oath, friends, and that's the reason the text gives.

The answer is Merab. The text says David took "…the five sons whom Merab daughter of Saul had borne to Adriel son of Barzillai the Meholathite." Merab was one of Saul's daughters. Along with Rizpah's two sons, that makes the seven. Keep the names straight, friends, there's a lot of them.

The answer is five. Two plus five is seven, and that matches what the Gibeonites asked for. The text says David took "…the five sons whom Merab daughter of Saul had borne…" Rizpah's two were Armoni and Mephibosheth. Together, friends, they make the seven.

The answer is at the beginning of the barley harvest. The text says they were put to death "…in the first days of the harvest, at the beginning of the barley harvest." Harvest is usually a season of gathering, and here it marks a sorrowful day. Sometimes the Bible just tells us when, plainly, friends. It's a heavy moment, so I'll leave it at that.

The answer is birds by day and beasts by night. The text says Rizpah "…did not allow the birds of the air to rest on them by day, nor the beasts of the field by night." Rizpah was Saul's concubine, and two of the seven were her sons. She spread sackcloth on a rock and kept at it, day and night. I think this one hurts, friends.

The answer is True. The text says she kept watch "From the beginning of the harvest until the rain from heaven poured down on the bodies…" Until then, she did not allow the birds or the beasts to rest on them. The rain, friends, is where the text marks the end of her watch.

The answer is Saul and his son Jonathan. The text says David "…went and took the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan…" from the men of Jabesh-gilead. Saul was Israel's king before David (1 Samuel 11:15), and Jonathan was Saul's son. The text tells us this happened when David was told what Rizpah had done.

The answer is False. The text says, "…they also gathered the bones of those who had been hanged." David had the bones of Saul and Jonathan brought from there, and the seven were gathered along with them. Nobody got left out, friends.

The answer is Kish. The text says the bones were buried "…in the tomb of Saul’s father Kish." Saul and Jonathan were laid in the family tomb in Zela, in the land of Benjamin. A family tomb is a quiet, settled place to rest, friends.

The answer is that God answers their prayers for the land. The text says, "After they had done everything the king had commanded, God answered their prayers for the land." It started with David seeking the face of the LORD, and it ends with God answering. That's the story, friends, from the first verse to the last.
